system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- For GROUNDED, use "hold" when unreadable PDF symbols prevent verification; explain what is needed. Use fail only when the available evidence is sufficient to determine that the claim is unsupported. This hold rule takes precedence over the strictness rule. Judge other checks independently using their listed values; do not invent missing facts.
- Be strict within each check's allowed values. Do not turn an inability to verify GROUNDED into revise or fail; use hold as defined above.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail / hold]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom, including its specificity, causal force, assumptions, and certainty. pass = fully stated. revise = partly stated (the atom adds, drops, or strengthens something; say what). fail = not stated when the available evidence permits a judgment. hold = unreadable symbols prevent verification. For pass or revise, put the supporting evidence ids in cite.
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately. Evidence spanning more than three sentences is not by itself a reason to split or revise an atom.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge. fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = an isolated study finding, conjecture, or author-specific opinion, classification, or recommendation, even if attribution was removed. Explicitly scoped established facts about a formalism or architecture and conditional theoretical results remain eligible.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a topic whose assessable content is restricted to excluded study-specific findings or author-specific positions. A named formalism, system, or architecture is not disqualified solely for being specific if its scoped conceptual facts are source-independent.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}

CONCEPT: Reverse-mode tensor calculus
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: Einstein-notation tensor multiplication, the expression DAG, and adjoint rules for multiplication and unary-function nodes. Includes why matrix notation is insufficient.

ATOMS:
- CS-ALG-C03-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: Any multiplication of tensors A and B can be written in the generalized Einstein notation as $C[s_3] = \sum_{(s_1\cup s_2)\setminus s_3} A[s_1]\cdot B[s_2]$, where $s_1$, $s_2$, $s_3$ are the index sets of the left argument, right argument and result, and the sum runs over all indices that appear in an argument but not in the result.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0230-s17] C[s3] = ∑ A[s1]·B[s2], (2) (s1∪s2)\s3
    [CS-ALG-p0230-s18] where C is the result tensor and s1,s2, and s3 are the index sets of the left argument, the right argument, and the result tensor, respectively.
    [CS-ALG-p0230-s19] The summation is over all indices that appear in at least one of the two multiplication’s arguments A and B and are not present in the result tensor C.
- CS-ALG-C03-S1-02 | S1
  ATOM: Any expression can be represented as a directed acyclic expression graph (expression DAG) in which input nodes (no incoming edges) are the variables or constants and output nodes (no outgoing edges) are the functions the DAG computes.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0231-s21] Any expression can be represented as a directed acyclic expression graph (expres- sion DAG).
    [CS-ALG-p0232-s02] The nodes of the DAG that have no incoming edges represent the variables or con- stants of the expression and are referred to as input nodes.
    [CS-ALG-p0232-s03] The nodes of the DAG that have no outgoing edges represent the functions that the DAG computes and are referred to as output nodes.
- CS-ALG-C03-S1-03 | S1
  ATOM: In reverse mode automatic differentiation, derivatives are computed from the output nodes toward the input nodes of the expression DAG, and each node $v_i$ stores the adjoint $\bar v_i=\partial y_j/\partial v_i$ of the function $y_j$ being differentiated.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0232-s09] In forward mode automatic differentiation one proceeds in the same direction for comput- ing the derivative and in reverse mode in reverse order, i.e., from output to input nodes. ∂y j Each node vi will eventually store the derivative which is usually denoted as ¯vi, ∂vi where yj is the function to be differentiated.
    [CS-ALG-p0232-s10] This partial derivative is often referred to as ∂y j adjoint.
- CS-ALG-C03-S2-01 | S2
  ATOM: For a node $C=f(A)$ where $f$ is a general unary function with domain index set $s_1$ and range index set $s_2$, and the output function has index set $s_3$, the contribution of $C$ to the adjoint $\bar A$ is $\bar f *_{(s_3s_2,s_2s_1,s_3s_1)} f'(A)$.

    [CS-ALG-p0232-s13] where the multiplication is again tensorial.
- CS-ALG-C03-S3-01 | S3
  ATOM: Matrix notation is insufficient for derivatives of vector and matrix expressions: for $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m$ the derivative is a matrix in $\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$, but the second derivative is a third-order tensor in $\mathbb{R}^{m\times n\times n}$ that cannot be represented in standard matrix notation.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0229-s22] Furthermore, when computing derivatives of vector and matrix expressions, even matrix notation is not sufﬁcient to express all derivatives.
    [CS-ALG-p0229-s23] For instance, for function f(x): Rn →Rm, the derivative will be a matrix M ∈Rm×n.
    [CS-ALG-p0229-s24] But already its second derivative will be T ∈Rm×n×n, i.e., a third order tensor, which cannot be represented in standard matrix notation.
- CS-ALG-C03-S3-02 | S3
  ATOM: Even when a derivative is a tensor of order two, it may have no matrix representation; for example, when differentiating $f(x)=x^\top A x$ by the chain rule, the derivative of $x^\top$ with respect to x is not the identity matrix and is not representable as a matrix, though in Ricci notation it is the tensor $\delta_{ij}$.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0230-s03] And even in the two-dimensional case, i.e., when the derivative is a tensor of order two, it might have no corresponding representation as a matrix.
    [CS-ALG-p0230-s04] For instance, consider the sim- ple quadratic function f(x) = x⊤Ax, where x ∈Rn is a vector and A ∈Rn×n is a matrix.
    [CS-ALG-p0230-s05] When computing the derivative of f with respect to x using the chain rule, one has to compute the derivative of x⊤with respect to x, i.e., the derivative of a function that maps x to its transpose.
    [CS-ALG-p0230-s06] This is not the identity matrix.
    [CS-ALG-p0230-s07] In fact, it is not even representable as a matrix.
    [CS-ALG-p0230-s08] In the more powerful Ricci notation [39] it would be written as the tensor δi j.
- CS-ALG-C03-S3-03 | S3
  ATOM: Standard Einstein notation, which omits the output index set and sums over all shared indices, can represent only a proper subset of the multiplications representable in the $*_{(s_1,s_2,s_3)}$ notation; for instance, it cannot directly represent element-wise multiplication.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0230-s25] In Ein- stein notation the index set s3 of the output is omitted and the convention is to sum over all shared indices in s1 and s2.
    [CS-ALG-p0230-s26] However, this restricts the types of multiplications that can be represented.
    [CS-ALG-p0230-s27] The set of multiplications that can be represented in standard Einstein notation is a proper subset of the multiplications that can be represented by our notation.
    [CS-ALG-p0230-s28] For instance, standard Einstein notation is not capable of representing element-wise multiplications directly.
